instructions.name: create_admin_pool
docs: Creates an admin pool with specified fees and parameters.
This function initializes an admin pool, setting various fees and limits
that will apply to vaults created by this admin.
# Arguments
* `ctx` - The context for the admin pool creation
* `creation_fee` - Fee for creating a new vault
* `protocol_fee` - Fee for using the protocol
* `trading_fee` - Fee for trading activities
* `money_management_fee_max` - Maximum fee for managing money in vaults
* `performance_fee_max` - Maximum performance-based fee
* `withdraw_cooldown_max` - Maximum cooldown period for withdrawals
# Returns
Returns a `Result<()>` indicating success or failure of the admin pool creation

instructions.name: create_vault
docs: Creates a new vault with specified parameters
This function initializes a new vault with the given configuration parameters.
It sets up the vault's contribution limits, raise periods, raise amounts,
idle and withdrawal periods, and various fees.
# Arguments
* `ctx` - The context for the vault creation
* `min_contribute_amount` - Minimum amount that can be contributed to the vault
* `max_contribute_amount` - Maximum amount that can be contributed to the vault
* `min_raise_period` - Minimum period for raising funds
* `max_raise_period` - Maximum period for raising funds
* `min_raise_amount` - Minimum amount to be raised for the vault to become active
* `max_raise_amount` - Maximum amount that can be raised
* `idle_limit_period` - Period after which idle funds can be withdrawn
* `withdraw_period` - Period during which withdrawals are allowed
* `money_management_fee` - Fee for managing the money in the vault
* `protocol_fee` - Fee for using the protocol
* `performance_fee` - Fee based on the performance of the vault
# Returns
Returns a `Result<()>` indicating success or failure of the vault creation

accounts.name: money_manager
docs: Staging-only counterparty, and necessarily still a signer.
Unlike `jupiter_swap`, this instruction does not touch a real market: the
vault sends input tokens to the manager's ATA and the manager sends
output tokens back, simulating a fill. `transfer_to_vault` uses this
account as the SPL transfer authority, so the token holder must sign.
The delegate cannot replace it — an execution wallet holds only gas SOL,
never trading inventory. A delegate-initiated dummy swap therefore
carries two signatures, and `dummy_swap` proves the authorization path
rather than the unattended-execution property. `jupiter_swap` is what
exercises unattended trading for real.

accounts.name: trader
docs: Whoever is signing this trade: the vault's money manager, or its trading
delegate when one is set. Authorization is asserted in the handler via
`VaultPool::can_trade` — it cannot be a `has_one` because either of two
keys is acceptable.
This account also **pays** the SOL trading fee and any asset-registry
realloc rent. That is deliberate: if the delegate signed but the manager
paid, unattended bot trades would drain the manager's personal wallet and
fail whenever it ran dry.

fields.name: publish_time
docs: The timestamp of this price update in seconds

fields.name: prev_publish_time
docs: The timestamp of the previous price update. This field is intended to allow users to
identify the single unique price update for any moment in time:
for any time t, the unique update is the one such that prev_publish_time < t <= publish_time.
Note that there may not be such an update while we are migrating to the new message-sending logic,
as some price updates on pythnet may not be sent to other chains (because the message-sending
logic may not have triggered). We can solve this problem by making the message-sending mandatory
(which we can do once publishers have migrated over).
Additionally, this field may be equal to publish_time if the message is sent on a slot where
where the aggregation was unsuccesful. This problem will go away once all publishers have
migrated over to a recent version of pyth-agent.

types.name: PriceUpdateV2
docs: A price update account. This account is used by the Pyth Receiver program to store a verified price update from a Pyth price feed.
It contains:
- `write_authority`: The write authority for this account. This authority can close this account to reclaim rent or update the account to contain a different price update.
- `verification_level`: The [`VerificationLevel`] of this price update. This represents how many Wormhole guardian signatures have been verified for this price update.
- `price_message`: The actual price update.
- `posted_slot`: The slot at which this price update was posted.

fields.name: previous_delegate
docs: Previous delegate, or all-zeros when none was set. Lets the listener
mirror a re-point (delegate A -> delegate B) without re-reading chain.

fields.name: money_manager
docs: The vault's money manager, always read from `VaultPool` state rather
than from whoever signed. Points, PnL and fee attribution key off this,
so it stays the real manager even when a delegate executed the trade.

fields.name: trader
docs: Who actually signed this trade — the money manager, or the vault's
trading delegate. Appended last so existing field offsets are unchanged.
Without this, a delegate-signed trade and a manager-signed trade are
indistinguishable in our records: if a delegate key were compromised we
could not say which trades were the attacker's, and a manager disputing
a trade could neither be confirmed nor refuted.

fields.name: trading_delegate
docs: Optional second key allowed to trade this vault — and only trade.
Carved out of the head of `padding`, so the account's total size is
unchanged and **existing vaults need no realloc or migration**. Every
live account already holds zeroes here (verified against all 178 on-chain
`VaultPool`s), so they decode as "no delegate" the moment this ships.
All-zeros is the disabled sentinel rather than `Option<Pubkey>`: an
`Option` prefixes a discriminant byte and shifts every following field,
which would force exactly the migration this layout avoids.

types.name: VerificationLevel
docs: Pyth price updates are bridged to all blockchains via Wormhole.
Using the price updates on another chain requires verifying the signatures of the Wormhole guardians.
The usual process is to check the signatures for two thirds of the total number of guardians, but this can be cumbersome on Solana because of the transaction size limits,
so we also allow for partial verification.
This enum represents how much a price update has been verified:
- If `Full`, we have verified the signatures for two thirds of the current guardians.
- If `Partial`, only `num_signatures` guardian signatures have been checked.
# Warning
Using partially verified price updates is dangerous, as it lowers the threshold of guardians that need to collude to produce a malicious price update.
